speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Thank you, Chief Justice. Congratulations to all of you who've reached this very important goal after years of hard work and sacrifice. Mr. Chief Justice, Justice Torres, Judge Farsinas, candidates and guests. When I was thinking about what to say today, I was thinking back to when I was sworn in as an attorney. At that time, we used our brand new IBM Selectric typewriters that we liked because we could make corrections easier and there were no instant communications and no virtual platforms. And when I came to Guam in 1977, we had an almost dysfunctional phone system. So every law firm had a lot of messengers and lawyers would gather at the Superior Court to engage in settlement discussions because it was difficult to talk on the phone. The Superior Court was different than it is today. It wasn't really too busy. And you could go over in the afternoon if you had an uncontested divorce or a simple matter and find a judge on the bench who would entertain your case and you'd be done and on your way. And the preparation of briefs were challenging because we didn't really have a law library then and you had to knock on the attorney general's door and ask if you could use their shepherds and manually shepherdize your cases. So clearly the how of practicing law has changed a lot in the last probably 30, 40 years. But what does not change is what it means to join the bar and enter this noble profession. What you did today has not changed. I solemnly swear you took the same oath I did in 1976 and you became an officer of this court gaining privileges and assuming demanding responsibilities. You swore to support the Constitution of the United States and the Organic Act of Guam. Our oaths require us to remain honest and diligent in upholding the rule of law even when it is difficult, even when you feel cases have been wrongly decided, you must continue to support and respect the rule of law. And you promised to respect the courts and judicial officers. Gaining the trust of a judge is really important. If a judge trusts you and trusts your work, your time in the courtroom will go a little easier. They may not always rule in your case, but judges will know that you have honestly presented the best work you can. And you swore to conduct yourselves honorably as an attorney at law. And to me, that means to faithfully discharge the duties of an attorney. To maintain a client's confidences, to represent your clients competently and diligently, to uphold the legal process and seek improvement in the law and access to our legal system. Take care in what you do, take pride in it. Sometimes I'm just astonished at a sloppy brief that's been submitted to the Supreme Court where it's clearly not even been proofread. And you also have pleadings in commercial paper or whatever area of law you practice. And those have to be right too, or your clients face difficult transactional problems or lawsuits or other difficulties. One of the most difficult matters that I recall as a justice is getting a complaint from a member of our community, a father, who had lost custody and visitation rights with his children because his lawyer hadn't prepared for or attended the court hearing. So think about the consequences to your client if you're not careful, if you aren't conscientious. If promising to conduct yourself honorably, you promise to conduct yourself with integrity and civility. And this is a promise greater than using good manners. It is a promise that requires us to work together to achieve a fair system, a system that represents the needs of our clients first and foremost. In that same sense, we see what the oath of attorney is about. It's about divesting ourselves. I'm sorry, it's about devoting ourselves to the betterment of the profession and our island to ensure that the rule of law is upheld, to advocate honestly and with integrity, and to make the system a fairer, more representative, and more just place for us all. At times, it is overwhelming. And today we recognize that the burden we have threatens our health and wellbeing. So I ask you to make another promise to yourselves today. Promise to take care of yourself and live a balanced life. Challenge yourself to invest in the time it takes to properly care for yourself and your family if you have one. Being an attorney is daunting at times, but it is so worthwhile. I never regretted choosing this profession. Sure, I can think of days I felt beleaguered or worried or ready to abandon a difficult client. But mostly I think of the clients I was able to help, a juvenile in trouble, a parent seeking a way to a meaningful relationship with a child, or the clients whose businesses overcame difficulties and challenges because of what I was able to do for them. Being an attorney led me to unexpected opportunities of public service and participating in making the system fairer, more representative, and a just and compassionate place for all. I hope that all of you find the same fulfillment and joy that I have. Again, my sincerest congratulations on behalf of my colleagues and the judiciary of Guelph.
